outline.chapter_title: 1. Factual Background, Claims, and Procedural Setup
outline.description: This chapter introduces the employment relationship, the 2019 overtime-policy change, the Minnesota statutory claims Cohen asserted, and the unusual procedural posture created by Consilio’s post-suit payments and the parties’ stipulations. It also explains the appellate standard of review, which frames why the Eighth Circuit treated some issues as pure questions of law and others as unresolved jurisdictional questions.
subtopics: Consilio’s business model and Cohen’s work as a Minnesota-based hourly licensed attorney document reviewer
The July 2019 email announcing the new overtime policy and the elimination of premium overtime pay
Cohen’s 2020 putative class action under the MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA
The remedies sought: overtime pay, liquidated damages, statutory penalties, and injunctive relief
Consilio’s payment of overtime wages and liquidated damages to Cohen and similarly situated employees
The parties’ stipulations that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages he claimed
The narrowing of the dispute to penalties and related relief
The agreement to decide Consilio’s summary-judgment motion before further discovery or litigation
De novo review of summary judgment and the requirement that no genuine issue of material fact exist

outline.chapter_title: 2. The MPWA Issue: Who May Seek Average Daily Wage Penalties?
outline.description: This chapter explains the court’s interpretation of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act and why it concluded that Cohen, as a private employee-plaintiff, could not recover the average daily wage penalties he sought. The focus is on the relationship between the general civil-action provision and the specific wage-demand provision, and on the court’s use of text and statutory comparison to separate private wage claims from commissioner-enforced penalties.
subtopics: Cohen’s MPWA theory under Minn. Stat. §§ 181.171 and 181.101
The structure of § 181.171: civil actions, compensatory damages, and penalties only when the violated section provides them
The key textual question under § 181.101(a): whether the statute authorizes an employee, rather than the Commissioner, to seek penalties
The statute’s sequence: commissioner demand, ten-day nonpayment period, and commissioner authority to charge and collect wages plus a penalty
Why payment of collected money to the employee does not create a private right to collect the penalty
The employee’s reserved right under § 181.101 to prosecute a claim for wages, as distinct from penalties
The court’s use of Minnesota plain-language interpretive principles and supporting cases such as Allan and Milner
Comparative statutory reasoning: §§ 181.13 and 181.14 as examples where the legislature expressly lets employees collect penalties
The 'legislature knows how' canon, including Lagasse, and its role in the court’s analysis
The holding affirming summary judgment on the MPWA claim because only the Commissioner may seek § 181.101 penalties

outline.chapter_title: 3. The MFLSA Issue: Paid Wages, Remaining Penalties, and Article III Jurisdiction
outline.description: This chapter covers the most important unresolved part of the case: whether a federal court still has jurisdiction over Cohen’s MFLSA claim once wages and liquidated damages have been paid and only statutory penalties remain. It explains how the Eighth Circuit shifted from the merits to standing and mootness, relied on federal justiciability doctrine, and remanded because the record did not clearly show whether the challenged overtime policy continued or whether recurrence was impossible.
subtopics: Cohen’s stipulation that he had received all overtime wages and liquidated damages owed under the MFLSA
The parties’ agreement that any MFLSA statutory penalties would be paid to the Commissioner, not directly to Cohen
Why the court treated jurisdiction as a threshold issue even though the district court had granted summary judgment on the merits
Standing for each claim and each form of relief under Town of Chester
The relationship between standing at filing and mootness during the litigation under Sisney
Laidlaw’s principle that civil penalties can sometimes redress private injury indirectly by deterring ongoing or future violations
The voluntary-cessation doctrine and why a defendant’s changed conduct does not automatically moot a case
The unresolved factual question: whether Consilio’s allegedly unlawful overtime policy remains in effect
How the answer to recurrence affects whether Cohen retains a live personal stake in MFLSA penalties
Why the Eighth Circuit vacated, rather than affirmed or reversed on the merits, and remanded for the district court to determine jurisdiction
The special concurrence’s caution that standing itself may be doubtful under Laidlaw in this context
The concurrence’s additional point that attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest should also be revisited on remand

outline.chapter_title: 4. The MWTA Notice Claim and the Failed Request for Injunctive Relief
outline.description: This chapter examines the two remaining parts of the appeal: Cohen’s Minnesota Wage Theft Act notice claim and his request for an injunction requiring Consilio to rescind the 2019 overtime policy. The chapter shows how the court used waiver and pleading rules to reject these arguments without extended merits analysis.
subtopics: The MWTA theory: failure to provide the statutorily required notice of a change in terms of employment under § 181.032
Cohen’s criticism that the district court gave little attention to the MWTA claim
Why the Eighth Circuit declined to reverse: Cohen had stipulated he was fully paid and cited no meaningful statutory basis for civil penalties under the MWTA provisions invoked
The appellate principle that unsupported assertions without developed argument or legal authority are treated as waived
The separate request for injunctive relief aimed at rescinding Consilio’s overtime policy
The mismatch between the specific injunctive relief sought in the complaint and the different relief requested later in summary-judgment briefing
The rule that new claims or materially new requests for relief must be raised through an amended pleading, not an opposition brief
The court’s reliance on pleading doctrine and Rule 15 rather than the substantive propriety of an injunction
The result: affirmance of the dismissal of the MWTA claim and no appellate consideration of the newly framed injunction request

outline.chapter_title: 5. Disposition, Doctrinal Takeaways, and What Remains on Remand
outline.description: This concluding chapter synthesizes the court’s mixed disposition and highlights the case’s practical significance for wage-and-hour litigation under Minnesota law in federal court. It clarifies what the opinion definitively decides, what it leaves open, and the procedural lessons about statutory remedies, justiciability, and issue preservation.
subtopics: The final disposition: affirm in part, vacate in part, and remand
What is settled: no private recovery of § 181.101 average daily wage penalties under the MPWA on this theory
What is unresolved: whether Cohen’s MFLSA penalties claim remains justiciable in light of payment and any change to Consilio’s policy
The distinction between merits questions about statutory remedies and jurisdictional questions about standing and mootness
How stipulations can narrow damages issues while still leaving federal-court jurisdiction uncertain
The importance of identifying who receives a statutory penalty and whether that penalty can still redress the plaintiff’s injury
The consequences of underdeveloped appellate briefing and failure to cite legal authority
The procedural lesson that requested relief must track the pleadings unless the complaint is amended
Practical significance for Minnesota wage litigation involving overtime, notice statutes, penalties, and equitable relief
The district court’s likely tasks on remand, including the status of the policy, mootness, possible standing issues, and ancillary matters such as fees, costs, and prejudgment interest
